newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish vehicle output falls to five-year-low.
newsitem.headline: Turkish vehicle output falls to five-year-low.

text.p: Turkish motor vehicle production fell in January to a five-year-low, depressed by seasonal tax increases and a leap in imports prompted by a duty-free import scheme.
The Association of Automotive Industry (OSD) announced on Friday a 23 percent fall in vehicle output to 21,046 in January from 27,292 a year earlier.
Car sector analysts had expected low output because of an annual rise in the tax on motor vehicles, which encouraged a rise in car sales in December helped by sales campaigns.
"Sales, which are generally low in January because of the rise in vehicle taxes, fell to their lowest level in the last five years," the OSD said in a statement.
Car output dragged overall vehicle production down by 38 percent from a year ago to 12,136 units in January due to weak demand, the OSD said.

The woes of the domestic car industry have been exacerbated by a government scheme allowing Turkish citizens at home and abroad to import cars if they deposit 50,000 German marks ($30,000) at state Ziraat Bankasi.
The Islamist-led coalition's plan attracted over 20,000 applications in the first three months after its introduction.
Expectations of duty-free imports seriously hit domestic demand in late 1996 although the deliveries of the cars will not begin till June 1997.
The latest figures indicated that carmakers' sales initiatives were not sufficient to offset the scheme's impact on domestic sales, the car association said.
"Despite companies continuing to offer low interest credit and other attractive methods to the consumers, domestic car sales did not reach the desired levels," it said.

The 8.2 percent rise in car sales in January to 9,408 was purely due to an increase in imports which surged 142 percent to 3,249. Sales of domestic cars fell 16 percent to 6,159 in January, according to the assocation.
The 34.5 percent share of imports in total car sales compares with only a 15.4 percent share in January 1996.
Domestic car makers saw their output eroded in response to a sharp rise in imports from the European Union as a consequence of Turkey's 13-month-old customs union with the European bloc.
European cars sold in Turkey in January made up 61 percent of the total car imports, followed by Asian cars which made up 35 percent of the imports.
During 1996, the first year in which the EU customs accord was in effect, Turkey's car production sank 11 percent to 207,757 and compared to a record 348,095 in 1993.
In the same period, overall vehicle output firmed two percent to 325,467.
The surge in foreign competition has brought warnings from leading Turkish carmaker Tofas Turk Otomobil Fabrikasi of dire consequences for domestic industry.
Commercial vehicle output in contrast showed a continued positive trend in January.
